newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. furniture sales seen up in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. furniture sales seen up in 1997.

text.p: The U.S. furniture industry can expect improved sales in 1997, despite a lack of new product introductions, a leading industry analyst told the fall International Home Furnishings Market on Thursday.

"We believe we are now receiving the benefit of higher housing sales last autumn, and therefore, should continue to see furnishings sales pick up ...," Jerry Epperson of Mann, Armistead & Epperson Ltd told exhibitors and buyers during the opening of the nine-day furniture show here.
Epperson also said new merchandising opportunities were emerging as more people work at home and aging Baby Boomers gain more income to spend on better quality furnishings.

While construction starts on new homes and apartments have trended higher, they fell six percent in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.438 million, the biggest drop in 21 months, the Commerce Department said on Thursday.

The furniture industry suffered throughout the first half of 1996, initially from foul winter weather. Sales also suffered because debt-laden consumers were reluctant to spend on high-priced furniture.

"More than 60 percent of the furniture purchased is bought on credit," Epperson noted. "Major credit card companies got very aggressive and lowered standards, and that created problems because ... anything that disrupts credit affects our industry."

Furniture retail analyst Britt Beemer said the industry still has a long way to go "before it's customer friendly." He recommended exchanging deferred-payment schemes for 30-day satisfaction guarantees.
"Often consumers postpone buying furniture because they fear making an expensive mistake," Beemer said.

"This market there's not many new product introductions," Epperson noted, but added that any new items out there are also big. Noting the size of the new beds, he quipped, "It's like they're all being built for professional wrestlers."
Celebrity names are big too. Arnold Palmer's name graces a collection for high-end manufacturer Lexington Furniture Industries.
More than 70,000 exhibitors, buyers, interior designers, sales and media representatives, architects and suppliers come to High Point twice a year for markets in April and October.
